questions.stem: A logistics company routes about 1.5 million inbound customer emails per day into one of 12 queues. The prototype uses the most capable Claude model and hits 96% routing accuracy on a labelled set of 800 real emails, but finance says the per-email cost is unsustainable and the operations team needs each email routed within two seconds. Routing categories are well defined and rarely ambiguous. What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Move the routing job to the Message Batches API so every email is processed at the discounted batch rate overnight.
Keep the current model and shorten the system prompt and category definitions until the per-email cost falls within budget.
Run the existing 800-email labelled set against a smaller, faster model such as Haiku and switch if it meets the team's accuracy target.
Switch routing to the smallest available model now, since well-defined categories make this a simple classification task that does not need a frontier model.

questions.explanation: The workload is high-volume, latency-sensitive and fairly simple, which is the profile Anthropic's model-selection guide gives for a faster, cheaper model. The guide also says the most important step in changing models is a **use-case-specific evaluation set**, and the team already has one. Re-running those 800 labelled emails on a smaller model turns a guess into evidence. If accuracy holds, cost and latency both drop. If it doesn't, you know exactly which capability gap justifies staying on the larger model.

whyWrong.A: Batch processing is asynchronous and can take hours, so it breaks the two-second routing requirement. It is a cost lever for jobs that are not time-sensitive.
whyWrong.B: Trimming the prompt cuts some input tokens, but the main cost driver is running a frontier model on 1.5M simple items. It also risks accuracy without measuring it.
whyWrong.D: Right direction, wrong process. The conclusion may well be correct, but switching without re-running the labelled set means any accuracy regression ships unmeasured. Anthropic's guide makes a use-case-specific eval the first step when changing models.

questions.mindset: Pick models with evidence: re-run your own eval set on the cheaper model before you switch.

questions.stem: A due-diligence platform uses a lead agent that plans the investigation and writes the final risk memo. It spawns 20–40 worker agents per case, and each worker reads one filing and extracts a fixed set of fields. Every agent runs on the same frontier model. Token spend is far over budget. Profiling shows over 85% of tokens are spent in the workers, and the memo quality reviewers care about depends mostly on the lead agent's synthesis. Which change gives the BEST cost reduction with the least risk to memo quality?

options.text: Keep the frontier model for the lead agent and move the extraction workers to a smaller, cheaper model, after confirming extraction accuracy on a labelled sample.
Move every agent, including the lead, to a mid-tier model validated on a sample of past memos, so the whole system uses one consistent model and costs fall evenly.
Cut the number of workers by having each one read four filings at once on the frontier model, so fewer agent instances are created per case.
Keep every agent on the frontier model but lower the maximum output tokens on all of them so each one produces shorter responses.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's docs describe **combining models**: an orchestrator on a frontier model that hands bulk work to cheaper workers, so most tokens are billed at the lower rate. Here the spend sits in the workers and the quality-critical reasoning sits in the lead, so you downgrade where the tokens are and keep capability where judgement is needed. Checking extraction accuracy on a labelled sample first keeps the change evidence-based.

whyWrong.B: Validating on past memos does not change the economics: this downgrades the one component that drives memo quality to save money on a part that is only a small share of spend. A single uniform model is not a goal in itself.
whyWrong.C: Batching four filings per worker on the same expensive model barely changes the total tokens processed. It also packs more content into each context, which can hurt extraction quality.
whyWrong.D: Capping output tokens doesn't touch the input-heavy reading the workers do, and it risks truncated extractions (`max_tokens` stops). It is a blunt tool, not a model-fit decision.

questions.mindset: Spend capability where the judgement is; push bulk, well-defined work to cheaper models.

questions.stem: A product team runs a contract-review assistant on Claude Opus with adaptive thinking. Accuracy on their eval suite is comfortably above target, but median latency and cost per review are both about 40% higher than the business case allows. An engineer proposes moving to a smaller model family. Without altering the validated prompts and with the fewest changes to the existing setup, what should the architect try FIRST?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt asking Claude to keep its reasoning brief and commit to one approach rather than revisiting decisions, then redeploy.
Move to the smaller model family as proposed, then re-tune the prompts and few-shot examples until the eval scores recover.
Turn on streaming so reviewers see the first tokens sooner, treating the latency complaint as a perceived-responsiveness problem rather than a model-configuration problem.
Lower the effort setting on the current model step by step and re-run the eval suite at each level to find the cheapest level that still passes.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's model-selection guide names **effort** as a lever that trades intelligence for latency and cost *within one model*, and says tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. Quality is already above target, so there is headroom to spend. Stepping effort down while re-running the existing eval suite keeps the validated prompts and model and gives measured evidence. The qualifier "with the fewest changes" rules out a model migration as the first step.

whyWrong.A: Prompt wording can trim reasoning, but it changes the validated prompt, its effect is hard to measure, and Anthropic's guidance is to prefer lowering `effort` as the supported, measurable control on thinking cost and latency.
whyWrong.B: Switching model families may end up being right, but it means re-validating prompts and examples. That is the largest change available, not the smallest.
whyWrong.C: Streaming improves *perceived* latency (time to first token) but doesn't reduce total generation time or token count, so the cost overrun and the measured median latency both remain.

questions.mindset: Try the cheapest lever on the validated setup first: tune effort before you migrate models.

questions.stem: An architect is advising several internal teams on whether to start prototyping efficiency-first (begin with a fast, low-cost model such as Haiku and upgrade only if evals show a gap) or capability-first (begin with the most capable model and optimize down later). For which TWO workloads is an efficiency-first start the MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: An autonomous coding agent that refactors a large legacy monolith over several hours with little human supervision.
Inline suggestions in a support console that must appear while the agent is still typing, at very high request volume.
A scientific analysis assistant where a wrong conclusion is costly and accuracy clearly outweighs per-request cost.
A multistep research agent that gathers sources and produces a finished, board-ready analysis document.
Tagging millions of product reviews per day with one of eight well-defined sentiment and topic labels.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guide recommends an efficiency-first start for **tight latency requirements**, **cost-sensitive** deployments and **high-volume, straightforward tasks**. Real-time console suggestions (B) and bulk review tagging with clear labels (E) fit that profile. You still validate with evals and upgrade only if a capability gap appears.

whyWrong.A: Long-running, high-autonomy agentic coding is the guide's example of where to start capability-first, because errors compound over many steps.
whyWrong.C: When accuracy outweighs cost and the reasoning is complex, the guide recommends starting with the most capable model and optimizing down later.
whyWrong.D: Multistep deep research carried through to a finished document is a high-capability workload, so starting on the smallest model would likely waste iteration time.

questions.mindset: Match the starting model to the workload profile: fast and cheap for high-volume simple work, capability-first for complex long-horizon work.

questions.stem: A bank is building a voice assistant for card services. The voice platform needs the first words of a reply within about one second, or callers hear dead air. About 90% of calls are routine (balance, card freeze, travel notice). The remaining 10% involve disputes where the answer must apply several policy rules correctly. In testing, a fast model passes the routine eval set but scores poorly on the dispute eval set even with the full policy text in its prompt, while the most capable model passes both but rarely starts replying within one second. A stakeholder insists on the most capable model at maximum effort for every turn "because accuracy matters". Which design BEST balances the requirements?

options.text: Use the most capable model at maximum effort for every turn, and play a recorded hold message whenever the reply takes longer than one second to start.
Answer turns with a fast, low-latency model and streaming, and hand dispute turns off to a more capable model, with the split checked against evals for both paths.
Use a fast model for every turn and add detailed dispute-handling rules plus several worked dispute examples to its system prompt instead of using a second model.
Run the fast model and the most capable model in parallel on every turn and speak whichever answer the most capable model produces when it finishes.

questions.explanation: The binding constraints are a sub-second start for most turns and higher reasoning quality for a minority. Anthropic documents multi-model strategies, including an executor that escalates hard decisions to a stronger model, and lists a smaller, faster model plus streaming as the main latency levers. Routing only disputes to the stronger model meets the latency SLA on the common path and keeps accuracy where it matters. Evals on both paths confirm the split works.

whyWrong.A: A hold message hides the SLA miss without fixing it, and maximum effort on routine balance checks wastes latency and cost on work that doesn't need it.
whyWrong.C: The stem says the fast model already fails the dispute evals with the policy text in its prompt. More rules and examples are the "add more prompt" trap when a known subset needs a different capability tier.
whyWrong.D: This doubles cost on every turn and still waits for the slow model before speaking, so it fails the latency requirement. It is over-engineered with no benefit.

questions.mindset: Design to the binding constraint: a fast default path, with escalation to capability only where the task demands it.

questions.stem: A marketing team uses Claude to turn engineering changelogs into customer-facing release notes. The system prompt describes the house style in two paragraphs ("friendly, benefit-led, short headline, one-sentence summary, no internal ticket IDs"). Outputs are correct but vary a lot in structure and tone from run to run, and editors spend time rewriting them. What is the MOST effective next change?

options.text: Rewrite the style description in capital letters with stronger wording such as MUST and NEVER so the model treats the rules as mandatory.
Ask Claude to re-read its draft against the style description and revise it before returning the final release note.
Add three to five varied, approved release notes as examples in the prompt, wrapped in example tags, that show the target structure and tone.
Switch to a larger model, since stylistic consistency in creative writing depends mainly on how capable the model is.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompting guidance calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer **format, tone and structure**. Few-shot (multishot) prompting with 3–5 relevant, diverse examples, wrapped in `<example>` / `<examples>` tags so they are separated from instructions, shows the model what "house style" means in a way that abstract adjectives can't. The content is already correct, so this is a consistency problem, not a capability problem.

whyWrong.A: Shouting doesn't make an abstract description concrete. Current models follow instructions closely, and aggressive emphasis can cause overcorrection without fixing the ambiguity.
whyWrong.B: Self-review against the same vague description inherits the same ambiguity. It also adds latency and cost without showing the model the target.
whyWrong.D: The model already produces correct, well-written content. Style variance comes from an underspecified target, which a bigger model won't fix.

questions.mindset: Show, don't describe: use few-shot examples for format and tone consistency.

questions.stem: An IT helpdesk triage prompt includes four few-shot examples. All four are short, single-issue tickets, and three of them are labelled "password_reset". In production, Claude labels many long tickets that describe several problems as "password_reset" whenever a login is mentioned, and rarely uses the "hardware" or "access_request" labels. The label definitions in the instructions are accurate. What change MOST directly addresses the root cause?

options.text: Replace the examples with a varied set that covers every label, includes long multi-issue tickets, and shows how to pick the primary issue when several appear.
Remove the examples and rely on the accurate zero-shot label definitions, since examples tend to bias a classifier toward the labels and ticket shapes they show.
Add a sentence to the instructions saying the examples are illustrative only and must not influence how often each label is chosen.
Add ten more short password_reset examples so the model learns the precise boundary of that label and stops using it for other tickets.

questions.explanation: The examples teach unintended patterns: "short ticket" and "login mentioned means password_reset". Anthropic's guidance says examples should be **relevant** (mirror real inputs) and **diverse** (cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns). Rebuilding the set to cover all labels and the long, multi-issue shape seen in production fixes the skew at its source.

whyWrong.B: Few-shot isn't inherently biasing; badly chosen examples are. Dropping them throws away a reliable steering tool for format and judgement instead of fixing the sample.
whyWrong.C: Telling the model to ignore the pattern its examples show is a weak, unverifiable counter-instruction. The skewed examples still steer the outputs.
whyWrong.D: This makes the imbalance worse. More examples of the over-predicted label reinforce the skew. "More few-shot" is not the same as better few-shot.

questions.mindset: Few-shot examples teach every pattern they share, so curate them for diversity and coverage, not volume.

questions.stem: A claims-intake service asks Claude to summarize customer emails for adjusters. A new compliance rule says that summaries must never contain a full payment card number, and any violation is a reportable incident. The current prompt already says not to include card numbers and has five examples showing masked numbers. Spot checks still find an occasional unmasked number. Which change BEST meets the compliance requirement?

options.text: Add ten more examples with masked card numbers, covering unusual formats such as numbers split across lines or written with spaces.
Add a second prompt step that asks Claude to review its own summary against the card-number rule and confirm none are present before it is released to the adjuster.
Move the card-number instruction to the very end of the prompt, wrapped in its own XML tag, so it is the last thing the model reads.
Add a deterministic redaction and validation step in code that detects card-number patterns in every summary and masks or blocks it before delivery.

questions.explanation: Prompting techniques such as few-shot, tag placement and self-review raise the *probability* of compliance, but a reportable-incident rule needs a **guarantee**. Anthropic's own guardrail docs say these techniques reduce errors but don't eliminate them, and to always validate critical information for high-stakes decisions. A deterministic check in application code (pattern detection with a checksum, then masking or blocking) runs on every output whatever the model does. Keep the prompt guidance to reduce how often the check fires, but the code gate is what meets the requirement.

whyWrong.A: More examples can lower the error rate, but they can't make it zero. This is the classic distractor of adding few-shot examples where a deterministic control is needed.
whyWrong.B: LLM self-checking is still probabilistic and can miss the same cases the first pass missed. It adds cost and latency without giving a guarantee.
whyWrong.C: Moving the instruction may change adherence slightly, but it is still a prompt-level nudge with a non-zero failure rate.

questions.mindset: If a failure is unacceptable, enforce the rule in code. Prompts lower the error rate; gates guarantee the outcome.

questions.stem: A benefits-eligibility assistant must apply six interacting rules (income bands, household size, residency, prior claims, age exceptions and a cap) to reach a yes/no decision. It answers immediately with no reasoning step, and about 15% of edge-case decisions are wrong, mostly where two rules interact. The model is a current Claude model that supports adaptive thinking, and a few seconds of extra latency is acceptable. What is the MOST appropriate change?

options.text: Add a line telling Claude to be extremely careful and double-check every rule, while keeping the response limited to the final yes/no answer.
Enable the model's built-in thinking at an appropriate effort level so it can work through the rules before answering, and verify the gain on the edge-case evals.
Add several few-shot examples that show only an eligibility question and its final yes/no answer, so the model memorizes the expected outcomes.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model gives the same answer to the same inputs every time and stops producing inconsistent eligibility decisions on edge cases.

questions.explanation: Multistep rule interaction is the classic case for chain-of-thought: the model does better when it can reason before committing to an answer. On current Claude models the supported way to do that is the built-in (adaptive) thinking, controlled by `effort`, rather than hand-written reasoning in the output. Anthropic notes that thinking adds latency and is worth it for problems that need multistep reasoning. The stem says latency headroom exists. Measure the change on the edge-case evals.

whyWrong.A: "Be careful" with no room to reason is a vague directive. It doesn't give the model a place to work through rule interactions, so the failure mode remains.
whyWrong.C: Answer-only examples show *what* to output, not *how* to combine the rules. For reasoning failures, examples need to show the reasoning, or the model needs thinking enabled.
whyWrong.D: Temperature affects randomness, not reasoning depth. A deterministic wrong answer is still wrong.

questions.mindset: For multistep reasoning errors, give the model room to think (built-in thinking or CoT), and measure the gain.

questions.stem: A content-moderation pipeline processes 400,000 short user comments per hour. Most are trivially safe, and a small fraction need careful reasoning about context and intent. After an engineer set every request to the highest effort level with thinking enabled, accuracy on hard cases improved slightly, but p95 latency tripled and cost exceeded budget. Which TWO changes are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Lower the effort level for the bulk of the traffic so the model responds directly on easy comments, and confirm accuracy on the eval set.
Raise max_tokens substantially so the model has more room to finish its reasoning quickly and return answers sooner on every comment.
Ask the model to write its full step-by-step reasoning into a JSON output field on every comment so reviewers can audit each decision.
Use a cheap first pass to flag ambiguous comments and send only those to a configuration with higher effort and deeper reasoning.
Add many more few-shot examples of safe comments so that the model spends less thinking time on them during each request.

questions.explanation: Reasoning depth is a cost and latency trade-off, so spend it where it changes the outcome. Lowering `effort` for the general flow (A) lets the model answer easy items directly, which Anthropic describes as the main lever on thinking cost. Routing only the ambiguous minority to a higher-effort path (D) keeps the accuracy gain on hard cases without paying for it on the 95%+ that don't need it. Both should be confirmed against evals.

whyWrong.B: `max_tokens` is a ceiling, not an accelerator. Raising it doesn't make reasoning faster and can allow even longer, costlier outputs.
whyWrong.C: Forcing written reasoning on every item adds output tokens, cost and latency, the opposite of the goal. On current models a prompt that asks for written-out reasoning may also be declined. Use built-in thinking.
whyWrong.E: Many extra examples make every request longer. Examples steer format and judgement, not how many thinking tokens the model spends.

questions.mindset: Treat reasoning as a budget: think hard only where it changes the answer.

questions.stem: A legal FAQ bot sends the same 12,000-token system prompt (role, policies and a reference glossary) with every request, followed by the user's question. Prompt caching is enabled with a breakpoint at the end of the system prompt, yet the usage metrics show almost no cache reads. The system prompt begins with the line "Current date and time: <timestamp to the second>". What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Remove the timestamp from the start of the system prompt and pass the current date in the user message after the cached content.
Switch the cache to the one-hour time-to-live option so that each cache entry survives for longer between successive requests.
Add three more cache breakpoints spread through the glossary so smaller sections of the system prompt can be cached separately.
Shorten the glossary to cut the number of tokens written to the cache on each request, since the 1.25x write premium is what is driving the cost.

questions.explanation: Cache hits need a **100% identical prefix** up to the breakpoint. A per-second timestamp at the very start makes every prefix unique, so every request writes a new cache entry and none are read. Put static content first and volatile content last: move the timestamp into the user turn, after the cached system prompt, and the 12k-token prefix becomes reusable.

whyWrong.B: A longer TTL doesn't help when the prefix is never the same twice. Each request still misses.
whyWrong.C: Every breakpoint after the timestamp still sits behind a changing prefix, so none of them can hit. More breakpoints don't fix bad ordering.
whyWrong.D: Write cost is a symptom, not the cause. The entries are written and never read because the prefix changes every time. Fix the ordering and the writes become reads at a fraction of the price; cutting the glossary may also remove context the bot needs.

questions.mindset: Stable content first, volatile content last: one changing token at the front kills the whole cache.

questions.scenario: An internal operations agent serves three roles (analyst, support, admin). Each role gets its own subset of the agent's 30 tools, which is correct least-privilege design. Requests carry roughly 9,000 tokens of tool definitions, then a 6,000-token system prompt, then the conversation. Prompt caching is enabled with a breakpoint after the system prompt.
questions.stem: Cache reads are rare even for back-to-back requests from the same role. Investigation shows that the tool list for a role is built from an unordered collection, so the order changes between requests, and each tool description has the requesting user's display name inserted for logging. What should the architect do?

options.text: Give every role the full set of 30 tools so that all requests share one identical tools block and a single shared cache entry across the whole agent.
Move the cache breakpoint onto the final user message so that the system prompt and conversation are cached together.
Build each role's tool definitions deterministically, in a fixed order with no per-user text, and record the user identity outside the prompt.
Switch to the one-hour cache time-to-live so that each role's cache entries stay alive through gaps in request traffic between user sessions.

questions.explanation: The cache prefix is built in the order **tools → system → messages**, and a change in tool definitions invalidates every level after it. A shuffled tool order and per-user text in descriptions mean no two requests share a prefix, even within one role. Making each role's tool block byte-for-byte stable (fixed order, no per-request values) gives one reusable prefix per role. Least privilege stays intact, and identity goes into logs and metadata where it belongs.

whyWrong.A: This trades away least privilege, a security control, to fix a cache problem that has a cleaner fix. Exposing admin tools to analysts is not an acceptable optimization.
whyWrong.B: Moving the breakpoint later doesn't help when the earliest part of the prefix (the tools) keeps changing. Everything after an invalidated level misses.
whyWrong.D: TTL isn't the problem. The prefixes differ on every request, so they would miss even if the entries lived longer.

questions.mindset: Caching needs deterministic prompts: stabilize the earliest layer (tools) and keep per-request data out of the prefix.

questions.scenario: A research firm runs a nightly job that scores 20,000 analyst notes against the same 40,000-token rubric and reference pack. The rubric is placed first with a cache breakpoint, and each note follows it. The job runs for several hours through the Message Batches API, and a separate real-time path scores urgent notes during the day by firing 200 requests in parallel at once.
questions.stem: Cache usage reports show many cache writes and few reads on both paths. Which TWO changes MOST directly improve cache reuse? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move each analyst note in front of the rubric so the unique content is processed first and the rubric is cached after it.
Use the one-hour cache time-to-live for the shared rubric, since batch requests can be processed well beyond five minutes apart.
Add the maximum number of breakpoints inside the rubric so that each section is cached on its own and hits independently.
On the real-time path, send one request first and wait for its response to begin before sending the parallel burst, so the cache entry exists.
Switch the real-time path to a larger-context model so the rubric and many urgent notes fit in one request and per-request caching is no longer needed.

questions.explanation: Two separate mechanisms are at work. **TTL:** the default cache lifetime is 5 minutes. Anthropic's batch guidance recommends the **1-hour** cache for shared context because batch items can be processed far apart in time, and notes that batch cache hits are best-effort, so a longer TTL raises the hit rate rather than guaranteeing it (B). **Concurrency:** a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins, so 200 simultaneous requests all miss and write. Warm the cache with one request, then fan out (D).

whyWrong.A: This reverses the right order. Putting unique content first makes every prefix different, so the rubric can never be a shared cached prefix.
whyWrong.C: Extra breakpoints don't fix an expired entry or a race on a cache that doesn't exist yet. The problem is timing, not granularity, and requests are limited to 4 breakpoints anyway.
whyWrong.E: Packing many notes into one request mixes independent scoring tasks and hurts per-note quality and traceability. It sidesteps rather than fixes the reuse problem.

questions.mindset: Cache hits depend on time as well as content: pick a TTL to match your traffic gaps and warm the cache before you fan out.

questions.stem: A finance-operations agent runs in an environment that supports Agent Skills. Its system prompt has grown to 70,000 tokens, because it contains 14 detailed procedures (month-end close, vendor onboarding, FX revaluation and so on), each 3,000–6,000 tokens long. Any single task uses one or two procedures. Teams say the agent sometimes blends steps from unrelated procedures, and every edit to one procedure means redeploying the entire prompt. What is the BEST way to restructure this?

options.text: Split the work across 14 specialist agents, one per procedure, with a router agent in front that classifies each request and forwards it to the right specialist.
Package each procedure as a separate Skill whose description states what it covers and when to use it, so only the relevant procedure is loaded for a task.
Compress all 14 procedures into a single condensed checklist that fits within 10,000 tokens and keep it in the system prompt for every request.
Keep the 70,000-token system prompt as it is and enable prompt caching on it, so the repeated procedures become much cheaper on each request.

questions.explanation: Skills use **progressive disclosure**: only each skill's name and description (about 100 tokens) sit in context until a task matches, and then the SKILL.md body loads. This removes the ~65k tokens of irrelevant procedures that cause cross-procedure blending. It also makes each procedure a separate module that can be versioned and edited on its own. Clear "what + when" descriptions are how Claude picks the right one.

whyWrong.A: A router plus 14 agents adds orchestration overhead, token cost and new failure points for what is a context-organization problem. It is over-engineered when on-demand loading solves it.
whyWrong.C: Heavy compression throws away the procedural detail that finance tasks need, and it still loads all procedures into every request.
whyWrong.D: Caching lowers cost and latency, but cached tokens still fill the context window. The blending and monolithic-edit problems remain.

questions.mindset: Load knowledge on demand: modular Skills beat one ever-growing system prompt.

questions.stem: A platform team publishes a "quarterly-report-validation" Skill. Two problems appear in review. First, Claude often fails to use the skill when users ask to "check the Q3 numbers before they go to the board". Second, when it is used, Claude writes fresh validation code every time, the results differ slightly between runs, and the long generated code fills the context. Which TWO changes BEST address these problems? Choose TWO.

options.text: Copy the full SKILL.md instructions into the agent's system prompt as well, so the guidance is present even when the skill does not trigger.
Inline every reference table and schema the validation needs directly into SKILL.md so that all of the material loads together when the skill triggers.
Bundle the validation logic as a script in the skill that Claude runs, so the checks are deterministic and only the script's output enters context.
Raise the model's effort level so it reasons more carefully about whether each user request might need the validation skill.
Rewrite the skill's description to state both what it does and when to use it, including phrasings such as checking figures before board review.

questions.explanation: Skill **selection** depends on the `description`, which is always in context and must say what the skill does *and when to use it*, in the words users actually use (E). For **deterministic** work, Anthropic recommends bundling executable scripts. Claude runs them, the script code never enters context, and only the output costs tokens. This gives repeatable results and a lean context (C).

whyWrong.A: This defeats progressive disclosure: the full procedure now costs context on every request, and the two copies will drift apart over time. Fix the trigger instead.
whyWrong.B: Reference material belongs in separate files that load only when needed. Inlining it bloats SKILL.md, and Anthropic's guidance is to keep SKILL.md concise. It also doesn't fix triggering or non-determinism.
whyWrong.D: Effort doesn't fix an under-specified description. Claude matches requests against the description text, so the description has to change.

questions.mindset: A skill is found through its description and made reliable by its scripts: write clear "what + when" triggers and move deterministic logic into code.
